planting.note: Plant on a lean, fast-draining slope with room for its mature arching habit; resume minimal watering at most twice a month after summer-deciduous leaf drop.

directions: A fountain-shaped chaparral shrub with a long spring-into-summer bloom of fragrant, snapdragon-like yellow flowers, this plant is deer-resistant and extremely low-water once established, making it a workhorse for dry hummingbird gardens. Site it where its mature arching habit has room without crowding, on a lean slope rather than flat, amended soil, since richness and extra summer water shorten its life. Don't mistake late-summer leaf drop for decline — it will releaf with fall rain.

planting.note: Plant with sharp drainage and some afternoon relief from the hottest sun, mimicking its native north-slope exposure; let sprawling stems lean on a nearby shrub or light stake.

directions: Vivid scarlet-red tubular flowers in whorled clusters from early summer into fall, later and redder than most chaparral penstemon relatives, decorate this sub-shrub with distinctive blue-green stems, a strong hummingbird and butterfly draw for dry Southern and Central California gardens. Stress-deciduous leaf drop in drought is normal, not failure. The late-season scarlet bloom makes it a good companion to spring-blooming chaparral penstemons for extending hummingbird nectar availability through fall.

planting.note: Plant in a dry, shaded understory such as beneath oak canopy; site behind evergreen structure, since the shrub is deciduous through both summer drought and winter cold.

directions: Unusual among its genus for thriving in significant shade, with specimens documented flowering well in nearly full shade under oak canopy, this Keckiella carries pale, purple-lined flowers and striking blue-green stems. It is the Keckiella to reach for when the planting site is dry but shaded rather than sun-baked, suiting oak-understory plantings better than most chaparral beardtongues. Established plants are long-lived and need essentially no supplemental water once past their first couple of seasons.

planting.note: Sow seed with 30 days cold-moist stratification in fall or early spring into rocky, sharply drained soil among rocks or at the base of a slope.

directions: A narrow, upright, mostly unbranched little shrub for rocky slopes in cooler, higher-elevation gardens, this Keckiella carries dull-purple, brown-streaked summer-fall flowers with a conspicuous hairy yellow staminode, a good nectar source late in the season when fewer natives are blooming. It is one of the few Keckiella that tolerates deep shade, so it can go into spots too dark for the full-sun chaparral species. Its narrow, mostly unbranched growth habit reads more as a vertical accent than a filler shrub.

planting.note: Sow seed (some pretreated with 30 days cold stratification, some untreated to hedge) onto rocky banks or retaining-wall tops; essentially no summer irrigation once established.

directions: A compact, low, trailing sub-shrub of the redwood belt and northern coast ranges, this Keckiella carries brick-red tubular flowers held through summer into fall, giving hummingbirds a late-season nectar source as other chaparral bloom fades. Its tolerance of serpentine and volcanic soils makes it useful for rocky banks or redwood-understory rock gardens where a sprawling rather than upright shrub is wanted. Overwatering is the most common cause of failure in cultivation.
